source.title: Learning to Focus: Focal Attention for Selective and Scalable Transformers
source.authors: Dhananjay Ram; Wei Xia; Stefano Soatto

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendices, but the figure graphics are not included in the supplied text; values shown only in figures cannot be read here.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation loss and downstream performance across model-size and training-token sweeps, but changes the attention mechanism rather than fitting or reproducing the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit power laws, report exponents, test predictions from smaller runs, or sweep compute budgets to find an optimal parameter/token split. It reports validation-loss plots and comparative scaling statements. Downstream-task results are relevant to V6; cited scaling-law findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture-method paper. It plots loss and accuracy against model size (400M–9.5B) and tokens (to 315B) only to compare Focal Attention with a baseline transformer. It fits no power law, makes no extrapolation, does no compute-optimal sweep and studies no shape effect at fixed parameter count. It reports no test of whether downstream accuracy tracks scale or loss predictably. Its scaling statements concern its own method's gap over the baseline, so it uses scaling as framing without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that Focal Attention scales better than a standard transformer in model size, training tokens and context length. They say it reaches the same accuracy with up to 42% fewer parameters or 33% less data, gives 17–82% relative gains on long-context tasks, and should be used from the start of training, since adapting a pretrained model recovers less benefit.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains LLaMA-style models with constant or learned temperature in the attention softmax and compares them with a standard-attention baseline; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies constant attention temperature, learned-temperature bounds, model size, training-token amount, and context length. It reports that constant temperature 0.4 performs best among the tested constant settings and that learned-temperature performance depends on its minimum-temperature setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Focal Attention (attention softmax temperature below 1) gives lower validation loss and higher average accuracy than a standard LLaMA-style transformer across 400M–9.5B sizes and 2.7B checkpoints to 315B tokens. The authors say the gap grows with scale and that it matches baseline with 42% fewer parameters or 33% less data. No fits or uncertainty are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural changes to attention can shift the loss and accuracy scaling curve (the offset or slope) relative to standard transformers.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the figure graphics and their numerical values. The study does not report uncertainty estimates for the scaling comparisons or fit scaling-law exponents. Results use a LLaMA-style architecture; the authors note that other architectures remain untested.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponent; loss curves are shown only as figures.
Depth and width co-vary with size; no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Text LM pretraining only; the long-context fine-tune is not analysed as a scaling law.
No analysis of whether downstream accuracy follows scale or loss predictably; there are only method-vs-baseline comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'supports' labels are removed, because the rows measure the study's own method against a baseline rather than downstream predictability. Downstream accuracy at the 315B point (Table 1: baseline 55.83, constant 58.02, learned 56.71) is a single-scale comparison. Appendix B's text contradicts Table 4: it gives 4e-3 as both the smallest and the largest model's learning rate, while the table lists 4e-4 for 6.7B and 9.5B. All scaling evidence is figure-only and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study plots validation loss against model size and training tokens, but does not test whether the curves follow power laws, fit exponents, or establish the stated several-orders-of-magnitude behavior.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
Depth and width scale together across model sizes; the study does not isolate architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
No tests of the claimed power-law form across other modalities or the listed training regimes.
The study reports downstream task performance across model-size and training-token sweeps, but does not fit or validate quantitative predictions from pretraining loss.
No analysis of scaling-law fit choices, exponent sensitivity, disagreement between laws, or curve bending.
